origins and historical notes on the aost: Origins and historical notes on the Aosta Valley

Inhabited since the fourth century BC by the people of the Salassi, the territory of the Aosta Valley was conquered by the Romans in 25 BC who founded Augusta Prætoria Salassorum, the current Aosta, where the imposing Arch of Augustus still stands in memory of that victory.

The roads built by the Romans, such as the Via Francigena that starts from here, favored the passage of the Goths, the Franks and the Lombards until the arrival of Umberto I Biancamano who, in 1302, transformed it into a duchy, granting the population ample autonomy.
Entered the Kingdom od Sardinia in 1847, Aosta Valley obtained the special status of the Italian Republic in 1948.

arch of augustus7: The Arch of Augustus in Aosta is not just a monument, but a bridge to a glorious era, a warning of the power and ingenuity of the Roman Empire.

porta prætoria5: The Gate is more that just a monument. It is a symbol of Aosta, a bridge that connects the present to the glorious Roman past of the city. A warning of the strength and tenacity that have characterized its history.

via francigena1:
The Via Francigena, which follows the Roman Consular Road of the Gauls dating back to the first century BC, connected Rome with northern Europe, favoring the exchange of populations and goods, but also the passege of military troops. Together with the Camino de Santiago de Compostela, it is one of the most important pilgrimage rountes in Europe. The original route was made in 990 by Sigeric, bishop of Canerbury, who had to arrive in Rome ro receive from the Pope (John XV) the 'Pallium', the stole of lamb the 'officially'oppointed him archbishop of Canterbury; from that moment it took the name of Via Francigena or Sigeric and become the itinerary of pilgrims heading to St. Peter's and, from here, to Brindesi (or Otranto) to embark from the Holy City.
The entire route is about 1800 km long. We will make the stretch from the Great St. Bernard Pass to Pont-Saint-martin. The route of about 90 km does not present morphological difficulties. With us we will have Enea Fiorentini, a member and friend of the GM section of Rome, who has been transferred to Aosta for several years. A great mountaineeur of the Francigena, in fact he has reconstructed and published a guide to the route. We also owe him the tiring work of identifying and booking accommodation and restaurants for this trip. Along the way we will come across small villages, historic centers such as Augusta Prætoria (Aosta) or Sait-Rhemy-en-Bosses, sites of archaeological interest dating back to Romanesque and medieval times, we will pass by famous castles (Quart, Nus, Châtillon) and churches rich in history. At several points we will walk on the furrows of the original Roman Road of the Gauls of the first century.
roman theatre1: The History of the Roman Theatre of Aosta is closely tied to the foundation of the city of Augusta Prætoria, ancient Aosta, by the Romans in 25 BC. This theatre is one of the most significant and well-preserved monuments from the Roman era in Northern Italy, showcasing the city's strategic and cultural importance within the Empire.
roman theatre3: The theatre was bilt during the 1st century CE, at the height of the city's splendor. roman theatre4: The theatre was part of the comprehensive Roman urban plan, which included the forum, baths, and other public buildings. It was designed for performances and theatrical representations, a key aspect of Roman social and cultural life.
roman theatre6: With th fall of the Roman Empire, the theatre, like many other structures of the era, gradually fell into disuse. During the Middle Ages, it was partially dismantled and used as a stone quarry for other constructions. Portions of the structure were integrated into later buildings.
roman theatre7: Over the centuries, the theatre was forgotten until archaeological excavations in the 19th and 20th centuries unearthed its monumental structure. Today, the theatre is one of Aosta's archaeological symbols and a major tourist attraction.
roman theatre9: Today, the Roman Theatre of Aosta is a visit-worthy archaological site, hosting cultural events and performances, thus maintaining a connection to its oringinal function. savoy castle2: Consisting of a central nucleus of roughly rectangular shape, flanked by five cusped turrents, each different from the other, the castle was designed by the architect Emilio Stramucci (creator of the neo-beroque decorations for the Royal Palace of Turin and the Quirinale in Rome) in medieval style, described as the 'Lombard style of the fifteenth century', widely used in France and Savoy, region of origin of the reigning sovereigns. castle of issogne1: Initially the domain of the bishops of Aosta, the property later passed into the hands of the Challant family. Over time the existing buildings were enlarged and united, until the radical transformation that took place between about 1490 and 1510 by Giorgio of Challant, prior di Sant'Orso, who made it a sumptuous residence for his cousin Margaret de La Chambre and her son Filiberto. It was then that the castel took on its current appearance, becoming a single horseshoe-shaped place, overlooking a large courtyard and an Italian garden, on whose high boundary wall important figures and heroes were painted; the portico on the ground floor was adorned with a series of lunettes frescoed with scenes of daily life and representations of shops, while in the center of the courtyard there was the famous wrought iron fountain called the Pomegranate, a symbol of prosperity. Also in that period, many interior rooms were decorated with frescoes, both in the reception areas, such as the Hall of Justice or the Chapel, and in the more privete rooms, including the oratories of Margurite de La Chamber or George de Challant. After the splendour of the sixteenth century, the residence began to decline progressively and in 1872 it was sold at public auction: purchased by the Turin painter Vittorio Avando, it become the subject of a careful restoration campaing that restored it to its former glory. Donated to the State in 1907, today the castle belongs to the Autonomous Region of Aosta Valley and has some elements of the original furniture and other furnishings redone at the end of the nineteenth century, which together with numerous objects of domestic use reproduce the late fifteenth-century setting desired by Avondo.

castle of verrès1:
Built on a rocky peak overlooking the village below, the castle is mentioned for the first tim in 1287 as the property of the De Verretio lords. An inscription carved in Gothic characters attests that it was Ibleto di Challant in 1390 who started the work that made the building take on its curent appearance. In 1536 René di Challant renewed the defensive apparatus of the manor, adapting it to the use of modern firearms. On this occasion, a wall was built equipped with gunboats, buttress spurs and polygonal offensive turrets, suitable for the use of the spingarde and cannons casr in the fief that the Count of Challant owned in Valangin, Switzerland; the entrance was made safer by the construction of the antegate with the drawbridge and the opening of loopholes. Nwe cross windows were also opened, in addition to the existing Gothic single-lancet and double-lancet windows, and new Moorish arched doors, of evident Spanish influence; the interiors were enriched with new furnishings. On the death of Renato di Challant (1565) without male heirs, the castle was forfeited by the Savoy. In 1661 Duke Carlo Emanuele II ordered the dismantling of the armaments and their transfer to the fort of Bard, a stategic point where the defense of the Aosta Valley was concentrated.
The Challants regained possession of the fortress in 1696 and kept it until the extinction of the family in the early nineteenth century. At that time the castle had been abandoned for almost two centuries: the roof, already partially collapsed, had been completely demolished to avoid the payment of the tax fee, so that the upper floors were exposed to the weather and overgrown with weeds. The rescue of this castle, as for those of Issogne and Fénis, is due to the interest of a group of Piedmontese intelectuals united by a passion for the Middle Ages.
castle of verrès2:
After passing th antegate that opens into the fortified walls, also accessible on horseback from the drawbridge, you come to the building intended as a guardhouse located in front of the entrance to the castle. Around this square room, the body of the building is arranged in a ring on three floors, connected by a monumental stone staircase set on flying buttresses. The geometric regularity buttresses. On the ground floor there are two large symmetrical halls that occupy the entire east and west sides of the castle, white the kitchen is located to the south. The eastern hall, probably originally used as a warehouse for artilley, is covered by a barrel vault. Of greater interest is the armory located to the west, with a pointed vault: it has two monumental chimneys with shaped jambs; the doubling of the walls and other clues that emerged during a restoration attest to the overlapping of several contruction campaigns.
On the second floo (not open to visitors) there are the service apartments, connected by a wooden staircase to the machicolation floor.

The castle of Ussel, located on an evident and steep promontory, looms from the south over the town of Châtillon.
Built by Ebalo di Challant in the mid-fourteenth century (a fact confirmed by dendrochronological analysis), the Castle of Ussel represents a turning point in Aosta Valley military architecture, In fact, we are in presence of the first example in Aosta Valley of a monobloc castle, the last evolutionary phase of the medieval castle, which marks the transition between the contemporary castle of Fénis and the rigid forms of that of Verrès.
castle of ussel2: After passing several times from the Cha;ants to the Savoys and vice versa, the castle was used as a prison, until it was completely abandoned. castle of ussel3: With a rectangular plan of considerable size, the castle has good masonry on the outside with a top band of blind arches, absent on the north side, and beautiful mullioned windows, all different from eac other, with floral andgeometric decorations. castle of fénis1:
Unlike the othe castles, built for war ad propection purposes, the castle of Fénis is not located on the top of a promontory, but an a slight hillock without natural defenses.
Combining the characteristics of the fortification with those of the fortification with those of the noble residence, the castle of Fénis was in fact the prestigious seat of representation of the major exponents of the Challant family, who equipped it with the imposing defensive apparatus, as well as elegant pictorial decorations, symbols of power and prestige.
The architecture of the castle of Fénis is the resul of construction campaigns that have takes place over the years: towers and crenellated walls were added towards the middle of the fourteenth century by Aimone di Challant to the pre-existing residence - a century earlier - of viscount Gotofredo II.
The castle of Fénis belonged to the lord of Challant pf the Fénis branch unit 1713, when it was sold to Count Baldassarre Castellar of Saluzzo Paesana. The events that marked the history of thar family led the manor to a slow degradation, a prelude to the abandonment that saw it transformed into a rural home: the rooms on the ground floor were used as stables, while the first floor was used as a barn.
The restorantion of the monument is due to Alfredo d'Andrade who bought the castle of Fénis in 1895 and, after restoring the most ruined parts, donated it to the State. Today the building is owned by the autonomous region of Aosta Valley.
castle of fénis2:
The castle of Fénis has a pentagonal plan; The corners have circular turrets, except for the south-west corner, which has a massive tower, and the south one, where the tower has a square plan. The keep is enclosed in a double ring of walls with guard towers connected by a patrol walkway.
Continue going up to the frrst floor, where you can see the chapel with the adjoining reception room, the chamber of directors, the noble kitchen, the dining room of the lords and the hall of justice.
The path ends in the internal courtyard, with the semicircular staircase surmounted by the valuable fresco depicting St. Georgie killing the dragon; Looking upstairs you can admire the wooden balconies decorated by a group of sages and prophets bearing cartouches on which proverbs and moral sentences in old french can be read. Remained almost intact from the moment of its construction, the Bard Ford represents one of the best examples of a berrier fortress of the early nineteenth century.

Already at the beginning of the sixth century A.D. there was a garrison in bard composed of sixty armed men who defended the so-called 'Clausuræ Augustanæ' the defisive system set up to protect the borders of the Empire.
In 1034 this system was defined as 'inexpugnabile oppidum, and this is one of the oldest refernces to a castle in Aosta Valley.
In 1242 the Savoy came into possession of the lordship of Bard, with Amadeus IV, driven by the insistence of the inhabitants of the area, tired of the abuses of Hugh of Gard who, thanks to the position of his castle, imposed heavy taxes on travelers and merchants. From that moment on, the castle always depended on the Savoy, who established a garrison there: in 1661 the weapons from the other Aosta Valley fortifications, including Verrès and Montjovet, were even concentrated in Bard.

The castle will then become the protagonist on the occasion of the passage of the French army in 1704 and above all the arrival of Napolen Bonaparte who, in May 1800, will find a defense army of 400 Austrians berricaded in the fort. The defensive structures of the were so effective thet the Napoleonic army took about two weeks to overcome them, succeeding only by cunning. The fort was then dismantled by Napoleon, to avoid further problems in the future.
What we see today is the renovation wanted by Carlo Felice who, in the midst of the Resoration, starting in 1830 made it one of the most massive military structures in Aosta Valley. Ay the end of the 19th century, the fort began to decline, first used as a penal bath and then as an ammunition depot. museum of fortifications and frontiers10:
The second part of he museum is housed in the rooms of the Opera Ferdinando Inferiore and is dedicated to the transformations that occurred between the end of the 19th and 20th centuries; it places the Bard Fort withis the system of 19th-century fortresses, reproducing scenographic reconstructions and scale models, aimed at highlighting not only the characteristics considered most representative of the fortifications in the Alpine arc, but also trying to make the Alps themselves the protagonists, the scene of a techonological evolution that led tham to become 'the frontier of Italy'. A story in the evolution of fortresses through the progress of weapons, and vice versa. The change in materials and construction techiniques, the gradual thickening of walls, the placement of forts in increasingly dominant places, the evolution of strategic methodologies and architectural solutions, all this is constantly brought back to the offensive capabilities of the enemy, and therefore to the possibilities of breakthrough by the besieging armies.
The theme of the militarized mountain is touched upon in the sections dedicated to the First and Second World Wars and to the Resistance, always aiming for the evolutive impact entrusted to a multimedia approach.
museum of fortifications and frontiers12:
The third and final sections poses a question with the aim of putting the visitor in a aposition to reflect on the path taken and on the meaning to be given to the term 'frontier': border or barrier? Obstacle or connecting feature?
An exhibition path is thus outlined that ransmits a complex and structured vision not only of the Bard Fort, but also of the historical, social, cultural and geopolitical context within which it is inserted in the different historical eras: a journey into the past that concludes with an extremely current reflection on the present.
The visitor is thus the protagonist of a dialogue with the place where he finds himself, in search of an identity, that of the Alps, in continuos evolution, which becomes a crossroads of the great events of the past and of that history of men made of simple memories and actions.

royal castle of sarre2: A royal residence that tells the story of the Savoy family and the hunting tradition of the royal house and the nobility. The castle is in a panoramic position and is located a few kilometres from Aosta and the tourist area of Gran Paradiso.
royal castle of sarre4: The castle stands in the Lalex area, on a promontory overlooking the Aosta plain above the state road to <Link href='/mountain/aosta_valley/mount_blanc' className='text-decoration-none color_link'>Mont Blanc</Link>, just beyond the crossroads for Cogne.
royal castle of sarre5:
Built in 1710 by Giovanni Francesco Ferrod di Arvier on the remains of a fortified house from 1242, after several changes of ownership it was purchased in 1869 by the king of Italy Vittorio Emanuele II, who renovated it and used it as a residence during his hunting trips in the Aosta Valley.
The royal castle of Sarre, which become part of the private heritage of His Majesty then became the headquarters used by the king of Italy for his expeditions in the valleys of Cogne, Rhêmes and Valsavarenche.
royal castle of sarre6: To host the first king of Italy, the residence underwent some modifications, including the raising of the tower and the construction of a new stable. Inside, the rooms were completely renovated and modernized. The curator of the Royal Palace of Milan was specifically charged with furnishing the house, which he accomplished by transferring the furnishings from other royal residences.
royal castle of sarre7: Even Vittorio Emanuele's successor, Umberto I (1844-1900) destined the Alpine castle for hunting-related uses.
royal castle of sarre8:
In the last years of his reign, umberto I paid particular attention to the residence of Sarre, promoting its internal renovation. Among the works carried out on that occasion, there are the important decorative campaigns of the monumental rooms, adorned with ibex and chamois trophies.
The castle was inhabited for holidays by Queen Maria José in the years following the monarchy.
royal castle of sarre9: In 1989 the Aosta Valley Region purchased the complex to restore it. The castle, which appears as a longitudinal body with a squere tower in the center, can be considered a museum of the Savoy presence in the Aosta Valley.
royal castle of sarre11: The visit route unfolds over three floors:
royal castle of sarre12: the ground floor is set up in a museum format and introduces the guided tour of the upper floors; some rooms are dedicated to the hunting theme and illustrate the territory, the management methods and the technical specificities of the royal hunts.
royal castle of sarre13: the first floor, which still retains the furnishings and the appearance it assumed in the second half of the 19th century, recalls the residential dimension of the castle's Humbertine phase; the rooms are presentd, with some exceptions, with the furniture documented in the 1890 inventory and with the textile furnishings described in the same inventory and reproduced on the basis of some original samples preserved in the State Archives of <Link href='/destinations/piedmont/torin' className='text-decoration-none color_link'>Turin</Link>.
royal castle of sarre14: the second floor, the exhibition presents a setting for chronological scans linked to the members of the Savoy dynasty who lived in the castle from the beginning of the twentieth century to the post-war period.
castle of aymavilles1: A one-of-a-kind castle that concentrates in its external appearance medieval and veroque phases, the result of the architectural initiatives of various members of the Challant family who over the centuries have adapted the building to the needs and testes of the time.
castle of aymavilles2: Book and buy your tickets online
castle of aymavilles3:
Castle of Aymavilles is located in the municipality of the same name in the Aosta Valley, on a hill surrounded by vineyards along the road to Cogne.
The castle has been the subject of a long and complex restoration project that began in 2000, involving multiple professionals for the design, studies and historical research, archaeological investigations and restoration.
The restoration involved both the architectural structure and the internal decorative apparatus, managing to enhance the particularities of the various building campingns and the numerous alterations that have occurred over the centuries.
Numerous anacdotes, surprises and curiosities have emerged from the past during archive research and during the works, all of which are now visible during the visit.
castle of aymavilles5:
The first mention of the castle dates back to May 1207. The castle began to undergo significant transformations starting from the 14th century, with the passage to the Challants, an important moble family of the Aosta Valley.
During the 15th century the castle was enriched by the four crner towers, a double wall and the construction of the top floor.
A large construction campaign dates back to the time of Joseph-Félix de Challant when, between 1713 and 1728, the spaces between the four corner towers were embellished with loggias, decorated with elegant stucco elements, while the interiors of the residence were significantly transformed and made more comfortable.
The creation of the terraced park helped give the castle the appearance of a modern stately home surrounded by greenery, completely losing that of a medieval defensive fortress.
During the 19th and 20th centuries, following various changes of ownership, the castle underwent numerous internal renovations, linked to its use first as a house museum by the will of the last descendant of the Challant family, Vittorio Cacherano della Rocca and later for summer holidays by Piedmontese and Ligurian families. In 1970 the castle became part of the assets of the autonomous region of Aosta Valley.
The green space of the castle extends over terraces sloping down towards the town and flanks, with its circular promontory shape, the surrounding hills used for growing vineyards. In spring and summer it hosts events and concerts.
The castle's appuntenances include the granze, once used for agricultural purposes, and the stables, the latter now used as a ticket office.
castle of aymavilles8:
The guided tour and miltimedia installations allow you to discover the history of the castle through the salient phases of its transformation, linked to the differnt families who lived there.
The museum tour unfolds on four levels:
castle of aymavilles9: Level I - the history of the families who have taken turs in the castle: on the ground floor the rooms illustrate the events of the Challant and Bonbrini families, the last owners of the castle before it was purchased by the autonomous region of Aosta Valley.
castle of aymavilles10: Level II - 19th century collectiong, from Vittorio Cacherano della Rocca Challant to the collection of the Academy of Sant'Anselmo: on the first floor the large hall represents the junction between the history of the castle and the birth of the collection of the Aosta Valley cultural association in the 19th century to which all the rooms in this section are dedicated.
castle of aymavilles11: Level III - the rooms of Madama Giovane and the collection of the Academy of Sant'Anselmo: the exhibition coexists with testimonies of daily life in the castle in the nineteenth century.
castle of aymavilles12: Level IV - the evolutionary phases of the castle and the wooden ceiling of the fifteenth century: the ettic, integrating with the still visible architectural testimonies, illusrtates the trasformations of the building over the centuries with the support of multimedia technologies.

castle of sarriod de la tour2:
The existance of the noble Sarriod family, politically linked but m=not related to the lords of Bard, is attasted since the 12th century. However, the origins of the castle, located in Saint-Pierre in a flat ares a short distance from the state road, remain obscore.
The oldest structure included the chapel and the centerl square tower (donjon) surrounded by a wall, a typical configuration of the Aosta Vally castles dating back to the 10th-12th century.
castle of sarriod de la tour3:
In 1420 Jean Sarriod had a real castle built where the tower known since the 14th century as 'turris Sarriodorum' already axisted, with representative functions by adding a series of bodies to the pre-existing dojon. The construction of the tower's spiral staircase (viret) and the insertion of the cross windows in cut stone characteristic of the 15th century Aosta Valley date back to this intervention. In 1478 Jean's son, Antoine Sarriod de la Tour, transformed the chapel dedicated to the Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist, on which occasion the external frescoes with the Crucifixion and Saint Christopher were created and the small bell tower was erected. In the north wing, on the ground floor, there is a large service romm with a wooden roof; on the first fool is the so-called 'hall of heads', which takes its name from the decoration of the wooden ceiling.
In the late 15th century the walls were equipped with circular and semi-cicular defensive towers and a new entrance to the castle was opened on the eastern side with a pointed portal and a sculpted archicolt bearing the Sarriod coat of armas.
castle of sarriod de la tour4:
The discontinuty between the levels in the various rooms attests to the various interventions that tooksplace over the followiong centuries. In the 16th century the wing that today constitutes the eastern façade was built, the tower at the noth corner dates back to the 17th century and some fragment of wall paintings and a stucco fireplace are from the first half of the 18th century.
The castle remained the property of the Sarriod de la Tour until 1923, when it passed to the Bensa family of Genoa. Since 1970 it has belonged to the autonomous region of Aosta Valley.
courmayeur1: One of the historic capitals of mountaineering and hiking, in winter it is a favourite destination for lovers of skiing and winter sports.
courmayeur2: Modern and functional ski lifts, ski areas for over 100 km of fun in the snow, an exclusive sitting that has few equals in the Alpine arc. Hare is Courmayeur, the 'pearl of the Alps', whinch links its fame to Mont Blanc and owes its 'tourist success' as one of the most renowned mountain resorts in the world to the highest mountain in Europe, for over 200 years. Nestled in a wide basic at 1224 metres above sea level, Courmayeur is the last Italian municipality you come across before arriving in France through the Mont Blanc Tunnel: a modern Alpine city, which developers around the ancient Church of Saints Pantaleone and Valentino and which today has its comercial and social hear in the central Via Roma. Born as a tourist resort at the and of the 17th century as a spa dor the cirtuas of its mineral water, it confirms its long tradition of hospitality at any time of the year, winth first-rate accommodation facilities and a wide range of sports that can be practiced in its Ferret and Veny valleys, against the backdrop of pricelles scenery. Loved by hikers and mountain enthusiasts in both winter and summer, it is known as the historic relics of the Casa delle Guide, home to the Museum Duca of the Abruzzi. The guardin of its ancient vocation as an agricultural community is the Bedoche festival, a folkloristic event linked to the rites of May, which today shares the celebrations of the patron saint in all the municipalities of Valdigne.
courmayeur3:
The history of sky lifts began in Courmayeur:
in 1908 the Donzelli, Gilberti and Lora Totino families built the first cableway. In 1939 this pioneering idea gave birth to the Mont Blanc Company, which built the cebleway from La Palud to Punta Helbronne. Soon after, the mountain, from a destination for a few climbers, become accessible to everyone.
courmayeur4: Today, with over 100 kilometres of slopes, Courmayeur is at the top of the list of winter sports in Italy and in the whole of Europe. The Courmayeur alpine ski area is in fact frequented by skiers from all over the world.
courmayeur5: For loves of Nordic skiing there is nothing better than spending pleasant days in Val Ferret which boasts slopes suitable even for inexperienced skiers. The are is partly flanked by a pedestrian path on the snow, to enjoy a walk in full nature a few kilometres from the town center. There are also various proposals for off-piste skiing, with the descent on the Toula glacier and those of the Vallée Blanche, which from the Mer de Glace glacier reaches Chamonix, on the French side of Mont Blank.
courmayeur6: If you are in Courmayeur, it is impossible to miss the crossing of Mont Blanc, the highest peak in Europe. Thanks to the Mont Blanc cable car, in just a few minutes you can reach over 2,000 meters above sea level. During the crossing, which starts at 1,300 meters at Pontal d'Wntrèves and reaches 3,466 meter at Punta Helbronner, passing through the internadiate station Pavillon (2,173 meters), you can enjoy a magnificent view of the glaciers and the great peaks of the Alps, visit the Saussurea Alpine botanical garden and the Mont Blanc crystal exhibition.
courmayeur7: Courmayeur is also one of the historic capitals of mountaineering and mountain hiking, whose history can be retraced at the Alpine museum 'Duke of the Abruzzi', housed in the House of Guides, in the center of the town. The museum collects documents, relics and climbing tools.
courmayeur8: Easily reachable in every season of the year (From France and the rest of Europe via the Mont Blanc tunnel, and from other Italian regions via the Aosta Valley motorway, which connects Torin to the Mont Blanc tunnel), Courmayeur is the ideal destination for anyone, even in summer, who wants to regenerate in contact with a cosmopolitan atmosphere, intimate but at the same time worldly and full of opportunities for meeting people.
monte rosa2: Monte Rosa, the second highest massif in the Alps after Mont Blanc, has a fascinating history that dates back millions of years and is closely linked to the birth of the Alps.
monte rosa4: Monte Rosa was formed between 30 and 40 million years ago, when the African place collided with the Eurasian plate, generating the great Alpine countain system. During this process, ancient marine rocks were lifted and transformed under enormous pressure, giving rise to the rocky structures that today constitute the massif.
monte rosa6:
For centuries, Monte Rosa has been shrouded in mystery and laged for the local populations. The glaciers and peaks often covered in perennial snow inspired fear, and the people of the valleys (such as Valsesia, Val d'Ayas, Gressoney and Macugnaga) told stories of spirits and forces of naure that inhabited those heights
In popular beliefs, the great expanses of ice were seen as inaccessible places, dominated by superior powers.
monte rosa8: Starting from the 18th century, with the spread of scientific interest in nature, Monte Rosa began to attrect naturalists, geographers and geologists, curious to study the glaciers and the conformation of the mountain.
monte rosa10: 1778: A group of crystal hunters and guides from Gressoney attempted from the first time to reach the peaks of Monte Rosa, probably reaching the Lys pass.
monte rosa11: 1801: There are reports of more arganized, but unsuccessful, scientific exploration towards the main peaks.
monte rosa12: 1842: The first great conquest: Giovanni Gnifetti, parish priest of Alagna Valsesia, togather with local guides, reached Punta Gnifetti (4,554 m) for the fierst time, today one of the most famous peaks.
monte rosa13: 1855: Dufourspitze (4,634 m), the highest peak in the massif, was conquered by an expedition led by the Englishman Charles Hudson with Swiss guides, marking one of the most important mountaineering feats of the time.
monte rosa15: In 1893, the Capanna Regina Margherita was inaugurated on Punta Gnifetti, commissioned by Queen MArgherita of Savoy. It was built to accommodate researchers and mountaineers, and became the highest refuge in Europe, serving as a scientific and meteorological observatory. This event marked the beginning of a period of intense moutaineering and scientific activity on Monte Rosa.
monte rosa16: Monte Rosa in the Twentieth Century
monte rosa17:
During the 20th century, Monte Rosa became one of the most popular moutaineering destinations in the Alps. The construction of new refuges, the development of the first cableways and the organization of international mountaineering expeditions made many of its peaks accessible, although it remained a difficult and severe environment.
Furthermore. it was subject of important glaciological studies, which contributed to the understanding of the dynamics of Alpine glasiars.
monte rosa19:
Today, Monte Rosa continues to be one of the most loved and frequented mountains by climbers, hikers and ski mountaineers. However, like all the Alps, it is deeply affected by climate change: its glaciers are repidly retreating, also modifying the classic ascent routes.
Despite this, Monte Rosa remains a symbol of Alpine culture and of man's challenge with nature, with a history that combines science, adventure and myth.
mont blanc1: The King of the Alps for unfrgettable summer and witer holidays
mont blanc2:
It is the highest mountain in the Alps and in all of Europe. At 4.807 meters above sea level, Mont Blanc is a true peradise for lovers of mountaineering and dowhill skiing.
The King of the Alps is part of the Mont Blanc massif, which extends for over 400 square kilometer between thw Aosta Valley and Haute-Savoie and includes very high peaks such as the Dente del Gigante, Mont Dolent and the Guglie di Chamonix.
mont blanc3: The main reference point for winter sports is the Mont Blanc - Courmayeur ski area with 100 kilometres of groomed and off-piste slopes, 33 slopes with various differences in altitude and 18 ski lifts that allow you to reach 2.755 meters above sea level. With the Skyway Mont Blanc cable car you can touch 3.466 meters to enjoy a unique view just a stone's throw from the sky.
mont blanc4: Those looking for some ideas for a summer holiday at the foot of the majestic Mont Blanc can count on kilometres of trekking and mountain bike trails strating from Courmayeur , such as the 170 kilometres of the Tour du Mont Blanc, or from Planpincieux with the so-called balcony of Mont Blanc, one of the most beautiful trails in Italy.
mount matterhorn2:
To represent a mountain, many draw a pyramid with its top reaching towards the sky.
The Matterhorn is just like that: a perfect mountain that stands out, isolated from the rest of the mountain range, in an enchanting valley, the Valtournenche.
mount matterhorn4: The Matterhorn (4.478 maters) was first conquered from the Swiss side on july 14, 1865 by Edward Whymper and other climbing companions, four of whom tragically died during the descent. A few days later, an entirely Italian climbing party, led by Jean-Antoine Carrel, climbed it from th Italian side. Even today, exper mountaineers from all over the world attempt to climb the Matterhorn. Trust the Alpine guides to make the most of this exciting experience.
mount matterhorn6:
If you are in Breuil-Cervinia and want to admire the Matterhorn up close then take the lifs up to Plateau Rosa, a skiing paradise, both in winter and summer.
The cable car allows you to reach ski area, but it is an experience not to be missed even for those who do not ski and want to enjoy the view, the clear sky and the crips air.
mount matterhorn7: The tourist area of Mount Matterhorn
mount matterhorn8: Going up the Valtournenche, which you enterat Châtillon, you can already begin to see the Matterhorn from Antey-Saint-André. The other municipalities overlook the valley from flat balconies: Torgnon and La Magdeleine, with their characteristic Alpine architecture, Chamois, reachable only by cable car or on foot, and Valtournenche which has in its territory the famous Breuil-Cervinia with its vast ski area that extends all the way to Zermatt, in Switzerland.
cervinia nature1: One of the most popular ski areas in Europe, in spring it transforms into an outdoor and active holiday paradise.
cervinia nature2: Everyone knows it as Cervinia, a ski resort in the Aosta Valley, renowned for the beauty of its landscapes and the variety of its ski slopes, but Cervinia is only the name given by its visitors to a much larger moutain area. The Breuil-Cervinia district, this is its full name, incates an area that extends from the 1,524 meters of the municipality of Valtournenche, to the 3,408 meters of the Plateau Rosà, and touches 4,000 meters with the Piccolo Cervino. And it also includes the 4,478 meters of the imposing Mettehorn massif, the symbolic mountain of the area, 'the perferct pyramid.'
cervinia nature3:
The name Breuil-Cervinia is not a coinsidence. In the Aosta Valley dialect, 'breuil' means 'land of many waters', a testament to the many lakes, streams and waterways that characterized the area of the original settlement of the town.
Breuil-Cervinia was in fact built more than two hundred years ago at the food of the Matterhorn, in the Breuil basin, an immense pasture that unit then could only be reached after hours of walking.
In the 1930s, the buildingd in the Breuil basin could be counted on the fingers of one hand, until 1934 when the Cervino Company was founded and the first Breuil-Plan Maison cableway was built in 1936, an event that gave rise to the development of waht is currently one of the largest ski areas in Italy and Europe.
cervinia nature4:
The Breuil-Cervinia Valtournenche Zermatt ski area is one of the largest in the Alps. It extends over valleys and two countries, Italy and Switzerland, with over 360 kilometers of slopes, so varied and numerous that thay allow you to ski alternating simple and more challenging routes.
In the area, not only Alpine skiing is practiced, thanks to the presence of a famous snowpark, the Indianpark of Cervinia - created in 2003 -, a freestyle area more than 400 meters long and 100 meters wide, aimed at snowboarders and freestyle skiers of all levels. In Valtournenche, on the other hand, there id the Wild West Park, a permanent skicross and jump track for freestyle.
cervinia nature5: Breuil-Cervinia is considered the ideal destination for cross-country skiing, with a 3 km loop, suitable for both beginners and experts Thanks to te high altitude (2,050 meters), the trail is naturally snow-covered and is open all qinter. Easy to reach, the trail is located at the entrance to the town, with Mount Cervinio in the background, surrounded by the Grandes Murailles chain, a series of peaks that never fall below 3,500 meters. In the Champlève area, in Valtournenche, there are two other loops, one 4 km long and one 6.5 km long in Maen.
cervinia nature6: The distinctive feature of the Breuil-Cervinia resort is undoutedly the possibility of skiing all year round. Part of the facilities of the Matterhorn Ski Paradise, the Italian-Swiss ski are that connects the resorts of Valtournenche, Breuil-Cervinia and Zermatt, are in fact located on the Plateau Rosà glacier which is always well covered in snow. Served by approximately 350 km of slopes, the plateau has many ki lifts, including a cable car that goes almost to the summit of the Piccolo Cervino.
cervinia nature7: Splendid, not far from the town of Cervinia, stands the Blue Lake, in which the imposing peak is reflected. Beyond the Blue Lake in the valley, Lake Goillet is also worth a visit, a suggestive artificial basin at 2,550 meters above sea lavel, closed by a dam, used for the production of hydroelectric energy and also for snowmaking on the slopes.
cervinia nature8: In summer, in addition to moutaineering, which makes the Matterhorn an internationally popular destination, it is possible to go trekking ad hiking. Paragliding and mountain biking are also very popular. For lovers of extreme sports, there is a exciting via ferrata and climbing walls.
cervinia nature9: For golf lovers, the valley is home to the 18-hole Cervinio Golf Club, one of the highest golf courses in the world (at 2050 m), aand founded in 1955. During the winter months the golf course becomes a cross-country skiing trail.
